body.text: The Interview: Gabe Bullard thinks tech convenience makes life worse

We're surrounded by apps and services that claim to make our lives run more smoothly and give us access to almost anything at lightning speed; from ordering takeaway, to streaming services, to "fast" self-serve check-outs. But what if these modern-day conveniences aren't what they seem?

In a new book, Against Convenience, US journalist Gabe Bullard argues they are making our lives, and the environment, worse, not better. And low-paid workers are bearing the cost. If we resist, he believes our minds and our bank accounts will benefit.
Bullard spoke with me from his home near Basel, Switzerland, where he lives with his wife in the village in which she was born.
What got you thinking about convenience in the first place?

The idea took root a while back. I was living in Washington DC and working for the local public radio station. A friend and I had been talking about doing a series of stories on the way apps were changing the city. We had seen people were using ride-shares to get around instead of taxis, that they were staying in Airbnbs instead of in hotels, and in such a tourist-heavy city like Washington that really started to make a difference in neighbourhoods.

Then this friend noticed someone using Taskrabbit, or a similar service, to hire someone to wait in line for a hot new restaurant, and the people who were paying pulled up in a ride-share. And a lot of that ends up relating back to convenience.

I wondered what might be the best possible framing around the way technology is changing our lives. I realised there is something that can be lost with convenience, or really something that is marketed as convenience ends up not being convenient, or has hidden side effects.
There are advantages of convenience too; we're speaking on a video call, for example. So, I really wanted to grapple with that idea and see if there was a case there.
Against Convenience is essentially an argument that our pursuit of faster and easier ways of doing things has hidden social and economic costs. What are the social costs?
I think one big social cost is a level of isolation; that the less that we need to leave the house for things or interact with people, the more isolated we can become.

Even if you're going out to get a coffee, if you're ordering ahead and just walking in, walking out, it's basically like going through the drive-through. You're interacting with a machine instead of a human being.

The other side of it, that I think in a larger sense can be more worrying, and I think will have longer lasting ramifications, is that so many of these things are catered exactly to us, like the algorithmic feed that's recommending what you watch, what you listen to, what you see, what you read, everything, how you shop, what you buy.

It's all being catered to us in a way that the real world wasn't, always so much under our control. And I think that there is something that happens over time as more of these interactions become not only predictable, not only isolating, but completely catered to us: I think it starts to warp the view of the outside world.

Because what happens to you when you stand in line and order in a coffee shop, it isn't necessarily built entirely around you, it's built to serve a group of people. And I think that it's very easy to see yourself as part of a community there.

In the book you talk about what happened when you stopped ordering coffee on an app. It was interesting you feel it had a positive impact not only on your day, because that little journey to get coffee was a joyful experience, but on your work as well.
Yeah, so it was shortly after the pandemic lockdowns, we needed to be a little bit isolated in the office.

I would dial up the app, order a coffee, work until the app said I could go get my coffee, go get it, come back and it was just sort of a hectic experience. It was really lonesome. I'm just kind of barely making eye contact with colleagues. And eventually, I realised, I don't like this. The coffee is just raw fuel that's powering my day and powering me sending emails or editing stories, just doing the drudgery of the day. And why should coffee be that drudgery as well?

So, I started going to a different coffee shop, asking people to come along. It was great. We could be outside. We could take our masks off and sit and chat outside while we enjoyed our coffee there, if we didn't feel like we had to rush back.

We bonded, we became better friends, better colleagues. I think we talked about a lot of ideas that wouldn't have come up if we were just sort of chatting on Slack from across a newsroom, that sort of thing. And also, the coffee was better.

You advocate for embracing a little friction in our daily lives. There's a quote I like towards the end of the book where you say: "Scrutinising a convenience can be the start of a new way of thinking about technology, consumption, and personal priorities." What else have you changed in your own life that's been revelatory for you?

I've stopped doing a whole lot of things either on my phone or through an app or even online whenever I can. For instance, it's getting cold here and I know that I need a new winter coat. When I do go online, I see a million ads for coats but I'm going to actually go to a store and buy one.

I've also started changing how I listen to music, especially after talking to musicians for the book and learning just how difficult it is for discovery, how difficult it is for them to get by, to make money. I've started buying more music, even if it's a digital download.
Essentially, I'm trying to avoid as many experiences as possible where something is done through a technological middleman like that.

I think that's been the longer history of a lot of digital technology in general, this idea that you stop paying for the thing that you want and instead pay for a tech company to provide it to you, and often that leads to the people who provide that service no longer getting paid very well.

I think that extends to a lot of other parts of life that I try to avoid. Working in media as well, I think there's this idea that news is free online, free if you're paying for the equipment to get there.
Another thing you advocate for is talking to strangers. What's the most memorable interaction that you've had with a stranger since writing the book?

There was one experience a couple weeks ago. I was in line at the grocery store, waiting to go to the human line. I had an interaction with a customer, we were just sort of chatting in general. She caught that my German wasn't that good and we had a small conversation about where I came from, what I was doing in the neighbourhood where I lived, that sort of thing. And it was nice.

I mention it now as a memorable thing. Maybe in a month I'll forget all about it. I think that's the joy of a lot of these interactions; they're really pleasant as they happen and then they fade away and you can just have another one. Life is full of little moments like that.

I talked with this psychologist, Jillian Sandstrom, who studies these minimal social interactions and she says, even down to waving at a stranger who you see, it's an acknowledgement that you're in a shared space, that this is another human being and they're acknowledging your humanity.

Something else she said that didn't make it into the book, was there's a reason they're called social skills. You build them up; you build up small talk. I will say I'm a very shy and awkward person, but the more that I have these small interactions, the more confident I feel talking about a book with someone on a Zoom call or talking to a stranger in line at the grocery store.
And if you don't use these social skills, they eventually start to atrophy, and experiences become a lot more awkward because it's something that you don't have the muscle to deal with.
This reminds me of my grandma. She turned these small interactions into an art form. I remember being with her as a kid and there was never a moment where she wasn't chatting to people in the street.

As a kid, sometimes I would feel so bored if I went with an adult to the grocery store and they started chatting with somebody and I would just think, why are you doing this? But now I find that it's something I really look forward to.
Have you read a book that's changed the way you think about a particular issue or yourself?

I just finished reading John Ronson's The Castle. It's in part about the male loneliness crisis. He talks about a man who was a successful YouTuber and had an advisor from YouTube advising him on how to hit certain keywords. It's a very small detail in the book, but it has me thinking a lot about how much gaming of what we see really does exist.

It's so easy to fall into this idea of even though the algorithm is curated for me, it's somehow reflecting a neutral idea, and it really does hide that larger network of what's behind it, who's serving you these things.
There's more responsibility from these technology companies than sometimes we want to give them for how the algorithm is shaped and what it's doing to overall taste and consumption.
I think you make quite a convincing argument in the book about how these technologies are making us lonely. Do you get the feeling there's a groundswell of turning away from convenience?
I do think more people are thinking about what this technology is doing to the world around us and what can or should be done on an individual or a community level.

I think the protests against data centres in the US is this recognition of the large footprint technology really has. And I think buried in some of the protests is also this question of, well, what is AI going to give me that I need right now? And that leads to thinking well, what do I actually need?

People are realising not only are they more isolated, but a lot of people are kind of bored. So much of what we end up getting fed through the distracting apps is not really that engaging. And it's not as fun as even a pretty mundane activity in the real world.

Here in Switzerland, there was a whole thing of eating pudding with a fork. It spread online but it was an in-person activity where they went to a park, they met at a certain time, they all had a little pudding cup and a fork and they like drummed on the lid and then sat and ate and hung out. And part of me is like, come on, that's so weird and just kind of chasing internet clout.

But I talked with somebody who had participated in one, they said, "no, it's just an excuse to hang out". It's app powered, but it's also an inconvenient thing to go meet in the park and eat a kind of soupy snack with a fork, which is kind of silly, but it is an excuse to socialise. And I think seeing things like that is pretty encouraging.
